bull.b: Royal Caribbean has rebuilt substantial earnings power, with strong margins, rising revenue, and net income of $4.4 billion TTM. This profitability provides resources to support fleet investments, strengthen the customer proposition, and absorb moderate demand or cost volatility over coming quarters.

Record pricing, strong booking activity, higher onboard spending, and expanding loyalty participation indicate durable customer engagement beyond ticket sales. Increasing pre-cruise purchasing and digital adoption can deepen ancillary revenue, improve guest monetization, and support repeat demand across brands.

Replacing floating-rate borrowings with long-dated senior notes due 2034 should reduce exposure to short-term interest-rate movements and improve maturity planning. Although debt remains substantial, this transaction supports greater financing predictability and may strengthen capital allocation flexibility.

bear.b: Royal Caribbean’s balance sheet has improved materially from peak leverage, but debt still exceeds twice equity. This leaves the company more exposed to refinancing costs and demand slowdowns, while interest obligations can restrict investment, shareholder returns, or strategic flexibility during weaker travel conditions.

Strong operating cash flow has not translated into positive free cash flow after investment and working-capital needs. The recent reversal from substantial positive free cash flow reduces internally available funding and is an important constraint when the company is also carrying elevated debt and funding fleet growth.

Year-over-year cost inflation remains a pressure on margins even with expected full-year cost discipline. If elevated operating expenses persist, Royal Caribbean may need continued pricing and onboard-spend growth merely to protect profitability, increasing sensitivity to weaker yields or adverse itinerary mix.
